title: Statistics for Analysts
description: Descriptive measures, distributions, sampling, confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests — the reasoning behind the number.

questions.prompt: Income data is strongly right-skewed. Which statement is true?
options: The mean is higher than the median
The median is higher than the mean
Mean and median are always equal
The mode is higher than both
questions.explanation: A long right tail pulls the mean upward while the median stays near the middle of the ordered values.

options: There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true
If the null were true, data at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
The effect size is 3%
The result is practically important
questions.explanation: The p-value is the probability of the observed (or more extreme) data under the null. It is not the probability that the null is true.

questions.prompt: A strong correlation between two variables proves that one causes the other.
questions.explanation: Correlation is association. Confounding, reverse causation, and coincidence all produce correlation without causation.

options: 95% of the sample lies inside the interval
If the study were repeated many times, about 95% of such intervals would contain the true parameter
There is a 95% chance the sample mean is correct
The interval contains 95% of the population
questions.explanation: The confidence level describes the long-run coverage of the procedure, not the probability that a particular interval contains the parameter.

questions.prompt: A value is 70 in a distribution with mean 50 and standard deviation 10. What is its z-score?
Which choices reduce sampling bias? Select all that apply.
options: Random sampling from the target population
A larger sample drawn from the same representative frame
Surveying only colleagues who are easy to reach
Stratified sampling across known subgroups
questions.explanation: Randomness and stratification improve representativeness, and a larger representative sample reduces error. Convenience sampling adds bias regardless of size.

options: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis
Rejecting a true null hypothesis
Using the wrong test statistic
Collecting too few observations
questions.explanation: Type I is a false positive: concluding there is an effect when there is none. Type II is failing to detect a real effect.

questions.prompt: What does the central limit theorem say about the sample mean?
options: Its sampling distribution approaches normality as sample size grows
It is always normally distributed for any sample size
It equals the population mean for every sample
It removes the need for random sampling
questions.explanation: For reasonably large samples, the distribution of the sample mean approaches normality regardless of the population's shape (with finite variance).

questions.prompt: Which measure is most resistant to extreme outliers?
options: Mean
Median
Range
Standard deviation
questions.explanation: The median depends on position, not magnitude, so a single extreme value moves it far less than the mean or SD.

questions.prompt: Repeatedly checking an A/B test and stopping when it becomes significant inflates the false-positive rate.
questions.explanation: Optional stopping without correction gives the test many chances to cross the threshold, raising Type I error. Fix the sample size or use a sequential method.
